title: Will GTA VI launch on PC soon after console release? GTA V on PS5 emulator already runs at up to 60 FPS - ixbt.games
content: Technology is gradually improving, and some players are hoping that Grand Theft Auto VI can be experienced on PC before its full release. After Sony's summer announcement about discontinuing PlayStation game discs, various projects to create PlayStation 5 emulators began to attract increased attention. Tech enthusiasts continue to work, and significant progress can already be seen with some games. For example, a user under the nickname BrutalSam published a short gameplay recording of Grand Theft Auto V on the KyTyPS5 emulator on a social network. About a month ago, when trying to play this Rockstar Games project, the emulator would freeze, but now it's possible to play the prologue – core mechanics and physics work, and the frame rate can be raised to 60 (overall, the game runs in the 40 – 60 FPS range). The test was conducted on a PC with AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT and AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D. The gameplay recording of Grand Theft Auto V on the PlayStation 5 emulator can be viewed at the following link. Some players hope that by the release of GTA VI, the emulator will be improved enough to play the new installment before the PC version's release. However, during the gameplay demonstration, the developers clearly indicated that the new game would be "heavier" than GTA V. Therefore, it's hard to imagine that KyTyPS5 will be improved enough in the remaining two months to comfortably play GTA VI on PC. Grand Theft Auto VI is scheduled for release on November 19 this year on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles. Rockstar Games and Take-Two have not officially announced anything about the PC version's release window, but rumors suggest that the gap between console and PC releases might be shorter this time. Players fear that Rockstar Games and Take-Two lawyers will have claims. Recently, a couple of videos by a modder under the nickname NokronDweller went viral in the Grand Theft Auto fan community. He published gameplay of his project called "GTA IV (GTA 3 PROJECT)" on his YouTube channel of the same name. He recreates the classic Grand Theft Auto III on the engine of the newer GTA IV. The videos he presented show a stylized main menu and alternative art with GTA III characters. Currently, his video diaries cover the early part of GTA III: from the escape scene on the bridge to meeting the first employers. This version uses the main mechanics from GTA IV, including a radar with GPS that indicates the route to the desired point. NokronDweller recreates both the missions themselves and their cutscenes. Players fear that "Rockstar won't like this" and lawyers may soon demand the project be shut down. The modder himself did not go into implementation details and has not yet published the files for public access. Grand Theft Auto IV is still popular to this day. Various mods are released for it, including an actively developing unofficial remaster – recently, the sensational NVIDIA DLSS 5 library reached it, and DLSS RR 4.5 (Ray Reconstruction) also became available. title: Prince William to represent King Charles at King Harald V’s funeral in Norway - UA.NEWS
content:
William, Prince of Wales, will represent King Charles at the funeral of Norway’s King Harald V, which will take place on September 9 at Oslo Cathedral. Buckingham Palace announced this, The Guardian World reports. William will be joined at the ceremony by his aunt, Princess Anne. She will attend the funeral in a personal capacity, as she is the godmother of Norway’s new King Haakon VIII. Under established practice, the British monarch does not attend the funerals of other heads of state. Therefore, Charles will be represented at the ceremony by his eldest son and heir to the throne, William. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. King Harald V died on August 28 at the age of 89. He ruled Norway for 35 years. Following his death, the country saw a broad outpouring of grief, while the late monarch was remembered as a people’s king known for his warm, informal style and sense of humour. The late monarch’s widow, Sonja, who now holds the title of queen mother, will also attend the funeral. After being informed of Harald’s death, Charles called him a dear cousin, close relative and friend, and noted his dedication to service, kindness, compassion and sense of duty. Queen Elizabeth II and Harald V were second cousins: their shared great-grandparents were King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra. In April 2025, William already represented his father at the funeral of Pope Francis at the Vatican. title: Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald V - The Guardian
content: Duty falls by precedent to William to attend service of late monarch, alongside Princess Royal, who is godmother to new king Haakon VIII The Prince of Wales is to represent his father at the funeral of King Harald V of Norway next week, Buckingham Palace has announced. William, the heir to the throne, will be joined by his aunt the Princess Royal, who is attending in a private and personal capacity as godmother of the new king, Haakon VIII. Norway has seen an outpouring of grief for the much-loved late monarch, who died on 28 August at the age of 89. Harald has been hailed as an inclusive “people’s king” who modernised the Norwegian monarchy during his 35-year reign. His funeral will take place on 9 September at Oslo Cathedral, with mourners including his widow, Sonja, now the queen mother. In keeping with precedent that the sovereign does not attend funerals of other heads of state, the duty falls to William, a future king, to represent his father and pay his respects at the service. Charles paid a touching tribute to his “dear cousin” and “much-loved kinsman and friend” after the news of Harald’s death was announced. In a message of condolence, he praised Harald’s “unwavering dedication” and his “kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades”. The late Queen Elizabeth II and King Harald were second cousins. They shared the same great-grandparents, King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra. In April last year, William represented his father at the funeral of Pope Francis in the Vatican. William and the now Princess of Wales carried out an official tour to Norway in 2018, dining with King Harald and Queen Sonja at the Royal Palace, where Harald described them as “family” and praised their support of the then Queen. The Norwegian sovereign processed into the banquet arm in arm with the pregnant Catherine, who was expecting Prince Louis and wearing a flowing Alexander McQueen gown, with the gesture mirrored by Sonja and William who walked behind them. William and Kate also spent time visiting the ski slopes with the then Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit, now the King and Queen.

FC Utrecht's match against Go Ahead Eagles was abandoned for good on Saturday evening. With more than an hour played and the score at 1-3, Utrecht fans misbehaved on several occasions and the game was not resumed. Go Ahead led 0-1 at half-time at Stadion Galgenwaard. When they went 0-2 and 0-3 inside the opening 15 minutes of the second half, Utrecht fans started throwing fireworks onto the pitch. Several loud bangs rang out. The fireworks seemed to have been set off from underneath a white sheet in the Bunnikside. Some exploded right next to the goal of Go Ahead goalkeeper Kjetil Haug. Referee Martin van den Kerkhof took all the players off the pitch, and the match stopped for about 15 minutes. Once play resumed and Utrecht pulled it back to 1-3 through Dani de Wit, cups were thrown onto the pitch during the celebrations. That forced another suspension. Following consultation with the local authorities, the decision was taken to abandon the match definitively. Under new head coach Anthony Correia, Utrecht had made a very disappointing start to the season with defeats to FC Groningen (2-1), AZ (1-4), PSV (1-6) and a draw against Sparta Rotterdam (3-3). At home to Go Ahead, who had taken seven points from their first four matches, the Domstedelingen were finally hoping to claim their first win. Led by Ángel Alarcón, Utrecht started well enough, but Go Ahead struck first after 18 minutes. Mathis Suray tried his luck from distance and the ball flew beautifully over Vasilios Barkas: 0-1. From there, Go Ahead took more control and carved out a chance for Stefán Sigurdarson. He swung over the ball in a promising position. At the other end, substitute Adrian Blake squandered a big chance shortly after half-time when he shot wide. Then it all happened quickly. Barkas first kept out an effort from Victor Edvardsen, but Søren Tengstedt tucked away the rebound for 0-2. Soon after, Edvardsen slotted home for 0-3 after a cutback from Tengstedt. De Wit pulled one back after the first temporary stoppage (1-3), but the match was then abandoned for good. title: Arteta v Alonso, part one: a desire for control and the theory behind the chaos | Jonathan Wilson - The Guardian
content: Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso prepare for an intriguing tactical battle in the first Premier League meeting between old friends Control v chaos. On the one hand, the forces of order, regimented, playing in precise patterns and, on the other, something darker, more visceral, a method that acknowledges the imperfection of the human soul, the unknowability of football in all its randomness; better, that second way says, to attempt to ride the fury than to believe it might be harnessed. When it began, a decade ago, that’s how the Pep Guardiola v Jürgen Klopp rivalry appeared. Apollo v Dionysius. Two fundamentally opposed ways of seeing the world. But in time, the two crept towards each other. Klopp moved away from the heavy metal of his Borussia Dortmund years to something more conservative. Guardiola experimented in multiple directions, slowly abandoning the possession-oriented idealism of his past to something less radical but also less predictable. The temptation, after the first two weeks of the season, is to cast Mikel Arteta and Xabi Alonso in a similar light. Arsenal are yet to concede a goal. They dominated the Community Shield from the first minute, beat a shambolic Manchester City 3-0 and gave the sense that they could easily have won more comprehensively had they been minded to do so. They were no more troubled in beating Coventry by the same scoreline in their opening league game and, while they were rather less dominant, they were still extremely comfortable against Aston Villa on Monday and had been slowly increasing the pressure when Bukayo Saka gave them the lead just before the hour. Arteta has become more controlling over his seven years at Arsenal, not just in his micromanagement but in his demands from his team. Tactical plans are sophisticated and negotiable only in the final details. In their third successive season of finishing second he spoke repeatedly of the need to reduce, to zero if possible, the xG of the opposition. If they have no chances, they cannot score, and if they do not score, they cannot win. Last season it was a refrain heard less often; Arsenal did reduce their opponents’ opportunities, conceding seven goals fewer than they had the previous season. There were those who criticised them on aesthetic grounds, bemoaning their reliance on set plays and occasional bouts of excessive pragmatism, but it worked. They were the best team and they won the league, in the end, fairly comfortably. All else is taste, subjective. Might, it will be asked, there be a more expansive approach this season? Might, with the burdens of yearning and doubt lifted, the insistence on control lessen? Might this be a breezier, a freer and easier, Arsenal? Might that even make them more effective in Europe, more capable of beating Paris Saint-Germain? Probably not. Arsenal played as they did in the Champions League final out of necessity, not choice. They were exhausted. Only three PSG players had played more than 2,000 minutes in the league last season; nine Arsenal players had – and given the relative strengths of the Premier League and Ligue 1, theirs were harder minutes. In such circumstances an open game is impossible. Accepting the role played by fatigue, in fact, has been one of Arsenal’s great strengths; last summer’s business was characterised by the accumulation of squad depth over acquisition of the very highest quality. This summer has been about upgrading where possible. They’ve seemingly done that well in midfield and at the back, although losing three players who can operate from the left wing while signing only Christos Tzolis seems a risk, even with Max Dowman likely to be more involved. It’s possible, likely even, that a more relaxed outlook will allow Arsenal to play with a greater freedom but it would be a surprise if the tactical emphasis were not still on control. Chelsea’s case is more complex; the sense of chaos of Alonso’s opening two games has surely not been deliberate. He is no Kloppite; his heritage is of John Toshack and Rafa Benítez, Vicente Del Bosque and Guardiola. Like Arteta, four months his junior, he came through the youth ranks at Antiguoko in San Sebastián; they are not so different in their formation. When Alonso won the league at Bayer Leverkusen, they had 62% possession. Although they pressed hard, they were not part of the high-tempo, high-turnover Bundesliga trend. Yet in beating Fulham 3-2, Chelsea had 38% possession, and in beating Brighton 4-3 they had only 26%. Game state is partly responsible. In both games, Chelsea had the lead early and could afford to allow their opponents the ball. The front three of João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers have excelled playing on the break. There have been glimmers of the sort of interactions Leverkusen produced, the modifications that prevent Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 from experiencing the blockishness that means the formation is more often a tool for counterattacking sides, most notably when Maxence Lacroix advanced from central defence to set up Rogers’ goal against Fulham. But they take time to develop; perhaps the idea for now, as patterns are assimilated, is to lean into the basic simplicity of shape, the security the two screening midfielders in front of the back three should offer. Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football The problem is, it hasn’t yet worked – although that may in part be down to personnel. Having sold Enzo Fernández without signing another central midfielder, though, Chelsea look short in midfield (in as much their bloated squad can look short of anything). If Roméo Lavia can remain fit, and if Reece James’s minutes can continue to be rationed, the issue should not be insoluble, but Moisés Caicedo’s knee problem complicates things, especially with Alonso seemingly unwilling yet to trust the 22-year-old Argentinian Valentín Barco from the start. Without Caicedo, that is not a midfield that is going to create much, and may struggle even with ball retention. It’s possible that on Sunday, in a game Chelsea are not expected to win, it is easier to maintain shape and discipline, that a destructive pairing works more naturally. Only by making the game a midfield slog to be decided by which team’s forward line can best exploit breakdowns can Chelsea feel they have an edge. That may end up looking like control against chaos, like possession against turnovers. It may even be so. But for Alonso that is a matter less of ideology than of expediency. South Africa’s power, confidence and energy swamped the All Blacks in the second half at Soweto’s FNB Stadium on Saturday. Yet, they still have a chance to share the series after the final Test in Baltimore, USA next weekend although they will have to do it without captain, and two-try scorer, Ardie Savea with a shoulder injury after having taken Marx’s head to the shoulder at a breakdown. He left the field and was replaced by Wallace Sititi. Coach Dave Rennie confirmed after the game that Savea will not travel to the USA. The Springboks’ scrum and lineout maul rampaged through the vital stages of the second half to reach a 29-17 lead and push the All Blacks into a pressure-laden catch-up game, which increased risks and saw close decisions go South Africa’s way. It was the most dominant South African performance of the series, with their power play taking the sting out of the All Blacks, never more than in the triumphant rolling maul that yielded a try for hooker Malcolm Marx 15 minutes from the end. Marx, No8 Jasper Wiese, lock Ruan Nortje, flankers Peter-Steph du Toit and Siya Kolisi were ever-present around the ball and increased the competitiveness of the breakdown. New Zealand did have a last-minute comeback when replacement hooker Samisoni Taukei’aho scored after a tap penalty move. While it drew them within five points, it could not hide South Africa’s dominant performance in key moments. The All Blacks lost skipper and No8 Ardie Savea, who scored two of their tries, late in the first half, and missed his experience and guidance. They also made more errors than was comfortable in such a tight game, errors that aided South Africa’s cause. New Zealand will look at the match statistics, where they had the better of the figures, and wonder why they couldn't convert them. They looked strong early, especially when running kicked ball back hard at the South Africans and gaining space on the flanks. Nine minutes into the half, Savea had the ball out wide and, in attempting to slip a pass to flanker Peter Lakai outside, the Springboks' first five-eighths, Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, stuck out an arm to impede the pass and was sin-binned. From the resulting lineout, hooker Asafo Aumua charged around the back to carry the ball close to the line where Savea was able to pick up the ball to score his 34th Test try. A mid-half burst of penalties conceded, starting from a scrum infringement and continuing downfield for three kicks to touch that found the Springboks on the All Blacks’ line, only to infringe themselves. However, they regained possession and worked the ball themselves to find second five-eighths Damian de Allende stationed wide. He beat wing Leroy Carter’s tackle and gave wing Kurt-Lee Arendse a chance to go over in the corner after 20 minutes. The All Blacks maintained their running play, and lock Sam Darry was fed into space and got into the Springbok 22m area. Working the ball wide, Savea threw a long pass to Carter, who took the ball down the sideline before the tackle. He released the ball, but Feinberg-Mngomezulu attempted to sweep it back. Unfortunately for him, Savea had supported and was able to take the ball to score his second try in the 25th minute. Five minutes later, Savea had to leave the field injured with a shoulder injury after having taken Marx’s head to the shoulder at a breakdown. He left the field and was replaced by Wallace Sititi. South Africa replacement fullback Manie Libbok then made an outstanding counter-attack run to be tackled just short of the line. Still, in the defensive response, first five-eighths Ruben Love was sin-binned for a cynical action in defence. That gave South Africa a five-metre scrum, which they used to roll the All Blacks back, but an offence led referee Nika Amashukeli to award a penalty try. The All Blacks lost centre Quinn Tupaea three minutes into the second half, but in working the ball from the lineout, Jordan was unable to hold the ball 15 metres out, which relieved the pressure on South Africa. A lift in tempo after replacements were introduced saw Roigard initiating more play, and after 55 minutes Jordan was in the line on the left from his right wing. He put a kick behind the Springboks' defence. Carter ran through to secure the ball and,, while tackled, lobbed it up for the supporting Jordan to take the pass and score. That broke the 12-12 impasse, but it was immediately negated after wing Ethan Hooker contested the restart and allowed South Africa to move the ball wide where centre Jesse Kriel beat Carter’s tackle and ran 25 metres to score. They added to that by unleashing their set-piece strength, first from a huge scrum after a long kick by Jordan went dead. From the scrum penalty, the Springboks set up a huge lineout drive that split the All Blacks’ pack and allowed Marx to go over under the posts to extend the lead to 26-17 with 15 minutes to play. South Africa 29 (Kurt-Lee Arendse, Jesse Kriel, Malcolm Marx tries;  Penalty try; Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu 2 con, pen) New Zealand 24 (Ardie Savea 2, Will Jordan, Samisoni Taukei’aho tries; Ruben Love con; Damian McKenzie con). title: Match Report: Black Ferns v South Africa, Rugby's Greatest Rivalry - All Blacks
content: The two sides played out a match that mirrored last year's World Cup meeting. Despite four yellow cards (15 against 13 at one stage) and a 17-7 penalty count, the Black Ferns found a way to prevail 52-20, at the FNB Stadium in Johannesburg, the largest venue to hold a women’s rugby international. They were pummelled in the scrums, conceding four penalties and struggled to defend the lineout drive, conceding two tries from that source. Catch up on all the action, stats and key moments in our Match Centre, Remarkably, however, when the Black Ferns were reduced to 13 players, they outscored the hosts two tries to nil. The Black Ferns started rapidly. A muscular maul forced South Africa to drag it down inside the 22. A quick tap followed, and the Springboks were stretched, with openside Elinor-Plum King going in unmarked to score. At Soweto's altitude, the pace was brisk early. After an exhausting passage of play, Hannah King fielded a clearance kick at the ten-meter mark in her own territory and delivered a spiral pass to Braxton Sorenson-McGee. She saw a splintered defensive wall, shimmed past two tacklers, and sprinted 55 meters. Sorenson-McGee was winded in the act of scoring. Hannah King slotted the conversion, making it 12-0 in as many minutes. This contrasted with the Rugby World Cup quarter-final where the Black Ferns made 95 of the first 98 tackles. Eleven of the starting XV for the Springboks were involved in that match. South Africa imposed their will for the first time in the 13th minute. Solid phase play earned a penalty, followed by a brutal lineout drive from the five-metre mark. South Africa’s most-capped hooker, Lindelwa Gwala, scored her 18th Test try in 42 Tests. At times, South Africa demolished the Black Ferns scrum. Their lineout wasn’t always reliable. Twice, chances were squandered. In the 28th minute, Black Ferns winger Mererangi Paul was yellow-carded for a deliberate knock-on. From the penalty, South Africa secured the lineout and the Black Ferns retreated, pushed back 15 meters. Pressed against their line, second five Aphiwe Ngwevu barreled ahead. Sylvia Brunt looked to have stopped the try, but the television match official ruled a clear grounding. Ngwevu has scored 17 tries in 35 Tests. The Black Ferns were at their most polished just before the interval. A 50 metre angled burst by Ayesha Leti-I'iga was only halted inches short. South Africa infringed and from the quick tap penalty loosehead Chryss Viliko barged through two for her fifth try in 24 Tests. With the ball in play and moving quickly, South Africa was reeling. Sorenson-McGee cantered in for her 17th try in 11 Tests after swift interplay between forwards and backs. It was 24-10 at halftime. Things turned pear-shaped six minutes after the break. Hooker Georgia Ponsonby was sin-binned in the 45th minute, with Leti-I'iga following a minute later. South Africa’s maul and scrum Kryptonite. Lock Vainah Ubisi barged over for a try. Instead of imploding, the Black Ferns rallied. In the 51st minute, South Africa tried to shift to the space. A fumble occurred inside their own half. Lock Maama Vaipulu made a strong run from the scrum. At the next ruck, Maia Joseph jinxed and hooped into a gap, crossing for her third try in 21 Tests. Ahead 31-15, the Black Ferns were unlikely to be passed. Joseph kept the tempo high, and a short pass on the Springboks' 22 saw Elinor-Plum King fend off a defender and zip 15 meters. Hooker Atlanta Lolohea, outside back Justine McGregor and Amarante Sititi were the picks of an impactful bench. Amarante charged through for a 73rd-minute try and almost completed a 40-metre break. Her older brother Wallace played for the All Blacks later in the day against South Africa. They are the first brother-sister combination to play a Test on the same day since Annaleah and Xavier Rush against Australia in Sydney in 1998. The Black Ferns won 27-3; the All Blacks lost 14-19. The Black Ferns' try to bring up a half-century was a beauty. Justine McGregor made an impactful carry and linked with Paul, who, after more twists than a Takapuna Pilates class, delivered a deft offload to lock Vaipulu. South Africa had the last say: Ubisi crossing for her 10th try in 28 Tests. Ponsonby (15), Liana Mikaele-Tu'u (14), Maia Roos (13), Mia Anderson (12), Vaipulu (11), and Veisinia Mahutariki-Fakalelu (10) were forced into double-digit tackle figures for the Black Ferns. Woman of the match Elinor-Plum King had eight tackles and a turnover to complement her strong carrying. South Africa captain and redoubtable tighthead prop Babalwa Latsha: “ The girls fought incredibly hard; our defensive sets were tested tremendously. We got some reward at the scrum. We keep building from here.” Black Ferns co-captain Geogira Ponsonby: “It’s a huge privilege to lead this team; at the end of the day, there are so many leaders in this team. They all stepped up. South Africa really brought it. They dominated in the set piece. This was a huge test for us; we needed that. It wasn’t pretty at times, but we stuck in there and scored some cool tries.” Zoe Naude (South Africa) refereed in her fifth Test. Since 2022, South Africa have achieved 27 of their 45 all-time victories. The Black Ferns have won 120 of 145 Tests, including their last six in a row. The Black Ferns' next assignment is France in Lyon on September 13. It is the first Test in the WXV series. title: Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing Ends This Year: Is a Mustang Really the Replacement? - Yahoo Autos
content: Autoblog and Yahoo may earn commission from links in this article. Cadillac will stop building the CT5 at the end of 2026, and the CT5-V Blackwing goes with it. What that removes from the American market is not a manual transmission and not a V8, but the version of them with a back seat you can reach through its own door. Two cars carry the combination forward, and they are both Mustangs. Whether that counts as a replacement depends entirely on which half of the Blackwing you were buying for. The 6.2-liter supercharged V8 makes 668 horsepower and 659 pound-feet, and it is assembled by hand, with the builder's name on a plaque bolted to it. Cadillac quotes 3.6 seconds to 60 mph with the manual and a track top speed beyond 200 mph. The manual is the standard gearbox and the ten-speed automatic is the extra. It starts at $98,900, and Cadillac is down to limited availability on what is left. View the 3 images of this gallery on the original article The first 250 cars sold out in minutes when it launched in 2021. The last of them are being built now. The end date comes from Cadillac itself. In a letter signed by Global Cadillac vice president John Roth, the company said the current CT4 and CT5 would be retired after the 2026 model year, with CT5 production running until the end of 2026, and that the legacy of the CT5 would continue as a next-generation combustion car in a future model year. That letter says nothing about V-Series, nothing about Blackwing, nothing about a V8, and nothing about a manual. A second-generation Blackwing has been reported by outlets citing sources inside GM, but Cadillac has made no public statement in the ten months since. Nobody outside GM knows whether the drivetrain comes back, and Cadillac has had ten months to say so. The closest thing to a comment came in February, when the car took another award and GM put up a quote from Brandon Vivian, the executive chief engineer running V-Series strategy. The win, he said, "validates what we've been doing with V-Series and V-Series Blackwing." Present tense, four months after the retirement was announced, and nothing at all about what follows. Nothing else on sale here pairs a V8 with a clutch pedal and four doors. Give up the doors and two cars remain, both parked in the same showroom. The GT does the job for $51,105 less, and it does it Cadillac's way: the manual is standard and the automatic costs money. On the Dark Horse, the faster car of the two, that order reverses. View the 2 images of this gallery on the original article The doors are the obvious one. If the point of the Blackwing was that it could carry four adults somewhere quickly and quietly and then do a track day on the way home, a Mustang manages the second half of that and not the first. Neither Mustang is supercharged. A great deal of the Blackwing's character comes from the blower, and a blown 6.2 delivers its power differently from a high-revving atmospheric 5.0, whatever the horsepower column says. The gap in that column is 188 horsepower and 244 pound-feet against the GT, and 168 horsepower and 241 pound-feet against the Dark Horse. Ford has not abandoned the manual as a default. On the GT it is the standard gearbox and the automatic costs extra, exactly as Cadillac arranges it. On the Dark Horse, faster and dearer, the automatic becomes standard and the Tremec an option. Ford treats the third pedal as the norm on its cheaper V8 and as a preference on its serious one. Ford has also said out loud what Cadillac has not. Asked at the Australian Grand Prix in March what happens to the Mustang's manual, chief executive Jim Farley said it would go "out of our cold, dead hands." At GM, Tony Roma, the executive chief engineer for performance cars, was asked the same thing about the Corvette at the 12 Hours of Sebring and said the company had "no plans to talk about a manual transmission." Nobody has put the question to Cadillac about the next CT5 and had it answered either way. Then there is everything about the Blackwing that has nothing to do with drivetrains: the interior materials, the ride quality on a bad road, the badge. A $47,795 coupe is not trying to deliver those. Related: Inside the Factory Where Cadillac Builds the Last Manual V8 Sport Sedan Cadillac has not spent this year behaving like a company winding a car down. It opened a one-off commissioning program, released a paint package in numbers it calls extremely limited, and in May built 26 cars for its Formula 1 debut with 685 horsepower, the most it has ever put in a Blackwing. V-Series had its best sales year on record in 2025, and GM says the division has since posted its best quarter and best first half ever. The used market has already priced this in. The 2022 Blackwing launched at $84,990. In the first week of September, a 2022 automatic with 18,000 miles was listed at $86,990 and a 2026 with 251 miles at $159,995. Options explain part of that, and these are asking prices, not sales, but four-year-old cars advertised above what they cost new is not how this market usually works. It has happened here before. Only 13 percent of second-generation CTS-V sedan buyers took the manual, according to Hagerty, and the manual cars are the ones worth money now. The people who made them rare were the ones who did not want the gearbox. There are two kinds of Blackwing buyer, and only one of them has been left with something to buy. If you wanted a V8 and three pedals, the answer is on sale now for roughly half the money, and the Mustang GT is not a consolation prize. If you wanted that combination with four doors, there is nothing, at any price, after December. If the doors are non-negotiable, buy now and expect to pay sticker or more. The successor is a rumor with no date attached. If they are negotiable, the Mustang will still be there next year, and it will not be scarce. Which of those two buyers you are is the one part nobody else can settle. This story was originally published by Autoblog on Sep 5, 2026, where it first appeared in the Features section. title: 2027 GAC Aion V review - CarExpert
content:
We use cookies to give you the best possible experience on the CarExpert website, to analyse our traffic and make sure that any advertising that is delivered is personalised to you. To find out more, visit our privacy policy. You've probably never heard of it, but if you're after an affordable electric SUV, the GAC Aion V should be on your list. If this is the car for you, we’ll compare offers from trusted dealers, handle the back and forth and manage your purchase from enquiry to delivery. It seems that every other week there’s a new Chinese brand entering the Australian market, and it can be hard for even automotive journalists to keep up. Tell someone there’s a new brand on the scene called GAC, or Forthing, or Deepal, or Lepas, and just watch their eyes glaze over as though you’re speaking some alien language. GAC arrived here last year with the Aion V you see here, a mid-size electric SUV, alongside the M8 plug-in hybrid people mover and petrol-powered Emzoom small SUV; the local lineup was expanded this year to include the small Aion UT electric hatch. The Chinese traces its automotive roots to the 1980s, although the present GAC Group was formally established in 1997. It established a joint venture with Honda in 1998, followed by one with Toyota in 2004. That should provide some assurance, as Toyota – with its vaunted reputation for quality and reliability – doesn’t trust others easily. Toyota even sells a restyled version of the Aion V in China called the bZ3X, so it clearly puts faith in GAC’s ability. By the way, GAC is an initialism, not an acronym, so you pronounce it as G-A-C. Don’t call it ‘gack’... the folks at GAC, uh, don’t like it when you do that. To keep things simple, GAC is selling vehicles from all of its brands under one GAC banner in Australia, much like rival GWM – and in sharp contrast to Chery with its confusing menagerie of brands. That means this vehicle, known in most markets as the Aion V, is a GAC Aion V; that also explains why it looks nothing like the Emzoom or M8. Oh sure, its styling is just as fussy as those two, but it’s just fussy in a different way. Credit to GAC for not designing another insipid Tesla Model Y or Land Rover Defender-inspired SUV, but we don’t think the Aion V will be winning many beauty contests. The Aion V competes in the affordable end of the mid-size electric SUV segment, undercutting top-sellers like the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7. The Premium opens the range at $42,590 before on-road costs, slotting below our Luxury tester at $44,590 plus on-roads. The most obvious rivals are the Geely EX5 ($41,990 to $45,990) and the Leapmotor C10 EV ($47,990 to $50,990 drive-away). Other sub-$50k mid-size electric SUVs include the MG S6 EV ($49,990 drive-away), and the recently launched Forthing Taikon 5 which starts at just $38,990 drive-away. To see how the GAC Aion V lines up against the competition, check out our comparison tool This mid-size SUV is brimming with features, and has seemingly everything but the kitchen sink… though it does have a fridge. The Aion V has a surprisingly upscale ambience and high-quality feel for something that costs less than $45,000 before on-road costs. You’re greeted, for example, with easy-entry front seats that slide back when you open the door, and then return to your set seating position once you sit down. Given its low price, perhaps the Aion V’s most impressive feature is the compartment in the centre console that can refrigerate, heat or even freeze items. You can, of course, use it as an ordinary centre-console compartment if you don’t want to leave items in the open storage area where they're visible to passers-by. However, we found the refrigerated compartment extremely handy, including on a visit to a cheese store far from home. It can also be left running even when the vehicle is off, only switching off when the vehicle’s battery reaches 10 per cent. This is the kind of feature usually found in $100,000-plus LandCruisers or much more expensive luxury cars, and has a level of adjustability that is staggering at this price point. The optional orange colourway in this top-spec Luxury may be an acquired taste, but you can’t say it’s not distinctive. Personally, I’m a fan. As with the smaller GAC Aion UT and a number of other Chinese models, the interior is minimalist, with little in the way of physical switchgear. You get a large 14.6-inch infotainment touchscreen and a slim 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, although there’s no head-up display even in this top-spec Luxury. We think it’s a little silly that there are no physical headlight controls, particularly when the Chinese government will soon require them. There’s still a stalk for the wipers and high beam, but any other headlight adjustments have to be made through the infotainment touchscreen. The touchscreen helpfully has an anchored bar at the bottom with shortcuts for functions such as temperature adjustment for each of the two front zones, as well as activation of the very high-resolution surround-view camera system. Speaking of the camera system, we love how it gives you the distance to an obstruction – for example, it’ll tell you how many centimetres you are from your garage wall as you get closer to it. There’s no swipe-down menu on the touchscreen like in many other cars, but there’s a shortcut menu that can be opened by pressing an icon on the footer. The infotainment system has quick response times and an exhaustive menu of adjustable settings, while wireless Android Auto booted up quickly and stayed connected without fail. One complaint about the touchscreen is that, on most screens, there’s no easy shortcut back to Android Auto or Apple CarPlay without pressing another button first. Poor English translations are kept to a minimum, although trying to switch off the driver attention monitor prompts you to ‘comfirm’ that you want to close it. Speaking of poor translations, using the voice assistant to close the sunshade also produces the unusual response, “Sun shades is turned off.” The voice assistant can be used for a number of functions and is reasonably intelligent, though sometimes it likes to linger. The lack of physical switchgear means you have to use the touchscreen to activate functions such as seat ventilation and massage. The front seats are very comfortable and decently supportive, and the massage system is excellent. It offers five programs and gentle, standard and strong intensity levels. If you adjust your seating position, a helpful prompt appears on the touchscreen asking if you want to save this position to memory. Everything feels solid and well screwed together. The only issue we observed was a tendency for the leather front seats to rub against the centre console as they were adjusted, resulting in a squeaking noise. The sides of the centre console are a mix of slightly soft and very soft trim, so it’s comfortable to rest your knee against it. Soft-touch trim is used on the dashboard and the upper sections of the doors, though some of these softer sections are clearly a thin layer of leatherette over a harder surface underneath. Regardless, it all presents well, and we particularly like the quilted leatherette accents on the door cards, which are subtly illuminated by colour-adjustable ambient lighting. There’s an unusual pair of bag hooks that initially look like buttons for the glove compartment, until you realise there’s no glove compartment at all. That’s a fail on GAC’s part, though otherwise cabin storage is good, including an expansive centre console shelf where you’ll also find a pair of USB outlets – annoyingly on the passenger side, though. The vanity mirrors have excellent illumination and unusual fold-down covers like you might see on a tablet case. Their lighting is almost like a ring light, so anyone using them to do their makeup should find them particularly useful. The digital instrument cluster is slim but has extremely clear and attractive graphics. It can display information such as tyre pressures, energy consumption and remaining range. However, the Aion V doesn’t display an exact battery percentage in its instrument cluster, just a remaining range. We’re not sure if this is to minimise your range anxiety, but it’s an unusual omission. A button on the steering wheel lets you toggle between different views, including one that displays maps from the embedded satellite navigation system. Step into the back and you’ll find the GAC Aion V extremely spacious, with ample room in every direction and a completely flat floor. The fixed panoramic glass roof bathes the cabin in light, but there’s a sunshade that’s thick enough to keep the cabin comfortable on a sunny day. This can be opened and closed via the touchscreen or by using voice prompts. There’s only a single USB-A outlet in the rear and no USB-C outlets, while the air vents are situated on the B-pillars. What appear to be controls for adjusting cabin temperature are actually controls for the refrigerator compartment. Don’t worry, though – if you don’t want your children fiddling with the temperature, you can lock them out via the touchscreen. Like the refrigerated compartment, the Aion V has another feature usually found in cars costing twice as much: a fold-out table on the back of the front passenger seat. It’s really neatly integrated into the seatback and is both a lovely surprise and a genuinely useful feature. There’s also a map pocket on the front passenger seatback. While the passenger seatback is largely finished in plastic, the driver’s seatback is finished in soft upholstery and has a more usable map pocket, albeit no clever tray table. If this is the car for you, we’ll compare offers from trusted dealers, handle the back and forth and manage your purchase from enquiry to delivery. Open the power tailgate and you’ll find a fairly average-sized boot with underfloor storage for charging cables and valuable items. A cargo blind is disappointingly not standard, although one is available, while dropping the rear seats doesn’t result in a completely flat load bay. If you were hoping for more storage under the bonnet, you’re out of luck – there’s no cargo compartment up here. To see how the GAC Aion V lines up against the competition, check out our comparison tool The Aion V is offered in Australia with only one powertrain and one battery. When we got into the fully charged car, it displayed 470km of range, despite an official WLTP claim of 510km. GAC claims energy consumption of 16.7kWh/100km, but on a loop comprising a mix of inner-city, suburban and highway driving, the Aion V used 14.9kWh/100km. Over the course of a week, including plenty of highway driving, this dropped to 14.5kWh/100km. My daily commute is predominantly highway, and I saw energy consumption of as little as 12.8kWh/100km. That’s pretty impressive. To see how the GAC Aion V lines up against the competition, check out our comparison tool The Aion V has a surprisingly polished feel, apart from some driver assist features that need further tuning. In many front-wheel drive EVs, the front tyres can be easily overwhelmed and you end up with wheelspin or torque steer unless you feather the accelerator. In the Aion V, however, there was virtually no wheelspin or torque steer. Only once or twice in the wet did we hear the tyres scramble ever so slightly. When I first got into the Aion V, I found the steering surprisingly heavy for a Chinese electric SUV and soon discovered it had been set to Sport. You can choose from three drive modes and adjust the brake response and steering effort, although changing these settings is more difficult than in many other cars. Switching to the Normal steering setting didn’t make the steering disconcertingly light or vague, as you might expect from a budget Chinese electric SUV. Instead, it retained a nice amount of weight and didn’t feel completely detached from the road, while still allowing the Aion V to be comfortable and easy to steer at low speeds. The ride also impresses, particularly for anyone coming out of a Geely EX5. Only on particularly patchy roads does it start to squirm a little. In almost all driving scenarios it feels comfortable and irons out the road surface, while its body control is hard to fault even over abrupt surface changes. Overall, the Aion V feels surprisingly well tied down and much better controlled than the floaty EX5. Performance is what you would expect in this segment. It has the instant torque of an electric SUV and no trouble getting up to speed or overtaking. At highway speeds, noise levels are fairly low in the Aion V, making this a pleasant long-distance cruiser. This may be due in part to the tyre selection, with the Maxxis VictraSport tyres proving to be good rubber for a number of reasons. You activate the cruise control not by pressing a button but by tapping the gear selector stalk down once; the Integrated Cruise Assistance, which combines adaptive cruise and lane-centring, is activated by tapping the stalk down twice in quick succession – don’t delay, or it won’t activate. Personally, I think a button would be better. If you pull the stalk down once to engage the regular adaptive cruise control and rely on the standard lane-keep assist, the system is fine. It feels smooth and not too obtrusive, and you can adjust the set speed using the knob on the right-hand side of the steering wheel. Integrated Cruise Assistance can follow the lane and negotiate curves, but it feels unfinished because any steering input causes the steering wheel to snap back in objection, giving it a very jerky feel. You obviously have to keep your hands on the wheel, but there were a couple of occasions when I felt the car was not exactly centred in its lane. And when I made a small corrective steering input, it yanked the wheel in protest. As far as systems in Chinese vehicles go, it’s not the worst – we've driven some Chery vehicles where this system is unreliable and constantly cancels itself. However, it’s not there yet and it’s not as good as systems in Japanese rivals, which is a common complaint we have with these systems in Chinese vehicles. The overspeed alert is infuriating because it defaults to on and can’t work out school-zone operating times, so it chimes when you’re travelling above a lower speed limit that applies at a different time of day. It’s a pain having to go into the vehicle settings menu every time you start the car and scroll down to cancel it, and we hope GAC comes up with a solution that allows you to quickly turn it off with, say, a long press of a steering wheel button like in Hyundai and Kia models. Changing your drive mode is also needlessly complicated. The driver attention monitor also chimed at me on a couple of drives, although it was generally good. The child presence detection, however, created multiple embarrassing situations. On a number of occasions, I’d lock the car and walk away and in less than 30 seconds the car would start honking because at some point I had opened and closed one of the rear doors after initially unlocking the vehicle. This system has a worthy purpose, but it’s horribly calibrated and it defaults to on. Here we have a Chinese SUV that’s actually quite pleasant dynamically, and yet like so many other Chinese SUVs it stumbles due to poor calibration of its active safety and driver assist technology. Fortunately, the Aion V’s biggest on-road flaws should be addressable through software updates. To see how the GAC Aion V lines up against the competition, check out our comparison tool The GAC Aion V has a five-star rating from independent safety authority ANCAP, based on testing conducted in 2025. GAC offers a long warranty in Australia, but doesn't yet have a capped-price servicing scheme. However, GAC does provide recommended service pricing. Most services have a recommended price of $199, though some carry a recommended cost of $640. To see how the GAC Aion V lines up against the competition, check out our comparison tool Among the growing number of mid-size electric SUVs under $50,000, the Aion V is one of the most desirable thanks to its mix of pleasant dynamics, a comfortable and well-appointed interior, and an enormous features list. We’d recommend this over a Geely EX5 or Leapmotor C10, for example, though all of these feature a compelling new competitor in the MG S6 EV. The GAC Aion V isn’t perfect. The styling won’t be to everyone’s taste. The safety technology needs calibration, particularly the Integrated Cruise Assistance and child presence detection. The lack of buttons inside the cabin grates, and there are some other omissions like the lack of a glovebox. We’d also caution GAC is a new brand to Australia and hasn’t had enough time to get some runs on the board. Nevertheless, GAC’s close involvement with Honda and Toyota gives us some faith in the Aion V’s long-term quality and durability, and the long warranty offers additional peace of mind. There's no capped-price servicing scheme yet like most rivals have, however, we expect one to be added in due course. While we don’t expect you to remember all of the new Chinese brands entering the Australian market, perhaps GAC is one you should commit to memory. Interested in buying a GAC Aion V? title: Sutton's predictions: Man City v Coventry City - Yahoo Sports
content: This is a tale of two Citys - one of whom has made the best of starts to the season, while the other has had the worst. Manchester City wiped the floor with Crystal Palace last week but it was their comeback to beat Bournemouth at the Etihad which felt bigger, because it was the beginning of a new era under Enzo Maresca. In contrast, Coventry City have had a terrible time. Not their 3-0 opening defeat at Arsenal, because they can forget about that, but they must feel so deflated after losing 1-0 at home to another promoted side in Hull City last time out. This game is more like the Arsenal one, in that no-one is expecting Coventry to get anything, but the upshot is they are likely to be left without a point or even a goal after their first three games. There were some doubts about Manchester City after the way they lost the Community Shield against Arsenal, but they look a different proposition already. Maresca has made more signings in the past few days, including Enzo Fernandez from his old club Chelsea for £125m. I've heard people question whether Fernandez is worth the big money that City paid, but Maresca knows him well and I see him as a great addition to their midfield. I said before the Bournemouth game I didn't think they could win the title without Rodri, but they have rebuilt their midfield now with Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi joining Elliot Anderson as new signings, and they have got real strength in there now. I like Erling Haaland's new haircut too. It suits him far more than a ponytail. He looks a bit rougher and tougher and I don't think Coventry will keep him out.

title: Sutton's predictions: Fulham v Crystal Palace - Yahoo Sports
content: Neither of these teams have got a point so far, as I predicted. On top of his side's poor start to the season, one of the problems for Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage will be dealing with Ismaila Sarr after he did not get a move to Liverpool before the transfer window shut. My worry for Fulham is they have become a Real Madrid feeder team, and their boss Alvaro Arbeloa has already got issues with his squad. He stuck the boot into his players after their defeat by Sunderland, questioning their mentality. A first win would be massive for both new managers, but I don't think either of them will get it here.

title: Sutton's predictions: Brighton v Leeds - Yahoo Sports
content: I am not really sure what to make of Brighton yet. They smashed Aston Villa on the opening weekend but then lost to Chelsea despite dominating possession in what was a really strange game. Leeds can be quite cagey on the road under Daniel Farke, but they are very good at what they do, and they will be a threat on the break. I am still going with Brighton to win because they are playing with freedom at the moment, but I don't see them keeping a clean sheet and this is going to be close.

title: Sutton's predictions: Brentford v Sunderland - Yahoo Sports
content: I was spot on with my predictions for both of these teams last week, but I still don't feel very confident about calling the outcome of this game. Brentford are a brilliant counter-attacking side who seem especially strong at home. I was erring towards backing the Bees to win, like they did in this fixture last season, but then had second thoughts. I backed the Black Cats to win their first two matches because they are a well-organised team, with plenty of physicality and also a threat up top. My concern for them is what happens when European football starts, but that hasn't happened yet. I don't see them losing this.

title: Commonwealth v. Kevin E. Goodman - norfolk.gov
content: NORFOLK, Va. — Kevin Eugene Goodman, 59, was sentenced in May to serve one year in prison and to complete the Community Corrections Alternative Program (CCAP) after he pleaded guilty to burglarizing and stealing from a residence last year. CCAP is a one- to two-year residential program operated by the Virginia Department of Corrections and is meant to prepare probationers who have taken responsibility for their crimes to return to their communities by providing them first with support such as academic opportunities, vocational training, and treatments for mental health and substance use disorders. On July 10, 2025, Mr. Goodman broke into the basement door of the victim's apartment on West Olney Road and stole the victim's bicycle along with various other items. The victim provided a security video showing the burglary and theft to Norfolk Police, and a detective who had previously arrested Mr. Goodman for an unrelated incident recognized Mr. Goodman from the footage and secured warrants for burglary and grand larceny. After Mr. Goodman was arrested in November, he agreed to speak with investigators and confessed to the burglary, claiming that he had stolen the items to support his substance abuse. While his case was pending in General District Court, Mr. Goodman expressed through his defense counsel that he wanted to take responsibility for his actions and that he intended to plead guilty when his case reached Circuit Court. Mr. Goodman waived his preliminary hearing, the Commonwealth agreed to withdraw his charge of grand larceny, and on May 26, 2026, Mr. Goodman pleaded guilty to burglary as charged. Mr. Goodman’s plea agreement called for a sentence of 12 months in the Department of Corrections followed by his completion of CCAP, with another four years suspended on the conditions that Mr. Goodman completes five years of supervised probation and uniform good behavior after his release. Judge Devon R. Paige accepted Mr. Goodman’s plea agreement and sentenced Mr. Goodman per the agreement. Mr. Goodman’s sentence was consistent with his Virginia Sentencing Guidelines. “Mr. Goodman broke into the victim’s home and stole possessions the victim had worked to buy and keep,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Ramin Fatehi. “Mr. Goodman will serve his prison sentence as punishment for what he has done. He will then join the Community Corrections Alternative Program with the goal of rehabilitating himself and acquiring the skills to help stay sober and out of the justice system. My prosecutors and I will continue to seek rehabilitative solutions that will help people who have done wrong to do better, thereby improving their lives, avoiding future victimization, and saving expense and heartache for our community as a whole.” Assistant Commonwealth’s Attorney A. Robinson Winn prosecuted Mr. Goodman’s case, and Norfolk Police Detective Kevin M. Gross led the investigation.

title: Court announces cases it will hear in December, including challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s - SCOTUSblog
content: The Supreme Court will hear a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and other semiautomatic rifles on Dec. 2. The oral arguments in Viramontes v. Cook County, which has been consolidated with Grant v. Higgins, headline the December argument calendar, which was released on Friday afternoon. Other highlights of the December argument session include cases involving the rights of parents to bring a lawsuit challenging a state law on care for runaway teens and Arizona election laws. The justices will hear seven separate arguments during the six days of the December argument session, which runs from Monday, Nov. 30, until Wednesday, Dec. 2, and then again from Monday, Dec. 7, until Wednesday, Dec. 9. Cutberto Viramontes filed the challenge to the ban on semiautomatic rifles in Cook County, Illinois, while gun owners and gun-rights groups challenged a similar law that Connecticut passed in the wake of the 2012 mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary in Newtown, Connecticut. In both cases, the lower courts upheld the bans against arguments that they violated the Second Amendment right to bear arms, prompting the challengers to come to the Supreme Court in 2025. After repeatedly considering the cases at their private conferences, the justices finally agreed on June 30 to weigh in. In International Partners for Ethical Care v. Ferguson, on Dec. 7, the justices will consider whether parents have a right to challenge Washington state laws allowing runaway teens to receive mental health care and treatment (including as to gender transitions of their children) at licensed shelters without parental consent. And on Dec. 8, the justices will hear oral argument in Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, a challenge to Arizona’s requirement that applicants using the state’s voter-registration form provide proof that they are U.S. citizens, which also raises the question whether a federal law, the National Voter Registration Act, allows states to remove noncitizens from its voting rolls within 90 days of a federal election. Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia (Nov. 30): Whether employees can bring lawsuits for sex discrimination under a federal law that applies to schools that receive federal funding. Wassily v. Blanche (Nov. 30): Whether noncitizens who receive asylum but whose asylum is later terminated can become lawful permanent residents or are instead always ineligible. Jouppi v. Alaska (Dec. 1): Whether the forfeiture of a $95,000 airplane – because a passenger was bringing beer into an Alaskan village where alcohol is prohibited – violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on excessive fines. Viramontes v. Cook County (consolidated with Grant v. Higgins) (Dec. 2): Whether bans on AR-15s and other semiautomatic rifles violate the Second Amendment’s right to bear arms. International Partners for Ethical Care v. Ferguson (Dec. 7): Whether parents have a legal right to sue, known as standing, to challenge state laws that (among other things) allow runaway minors seeking gender-transition treatments to be referred for services without parental notice or consent. Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota (Dec. 8): A dispute over (among other things) Arizona’s requirement of proof of U.S. citizenship to vote. Grand v. City of University Heights (Dec. 9): A religious-discrimination lawsuit brought by an Orthodox Jewish man against city officials who told him he needed a permit to host a prayer group in his home.
